t: The tanker left port with 22 crew members.
When the Coast Guard found it drifting,
there were 23 people on board.
I'm the Marine Inspector who was sent
to find out who the extra one was.
I counted them three times that night.
And the third time, I understood why nobody
on that ship would ever say the number out loud.
But it started six hours earlier.
My name is Daniel Reeve.
I'm 38 and I inspect ships after something goes wrong.
Collisions, fires, missing cargo.
Usually it's paperwork.
The vessel was the Halcyon Star,
a 90,000 ton oil tanker.
12 days ago, she left Rotterdam with a full crew list.
22 names.
Eight days ago, she stopped answering the radio.
This morning, a patrol aircraft
found her 400 nautical miles off the coast.
Engines idling, lights on,
drifting in a perfectly straight line.
The Coast Guard didn't want to board her.
They said the transponder
was still broadcasting the crew count.
And the count said 23.
A helicopter lowered me onto the deck at 6:12 p.m.
The pilot shouted over the rotors,
we'll circle for an hour, then we have to refuel.
Don't stay aboard past midnight.
I asked him why, he didn't answer.
He just pointed at the bridge
where the glass was fogged from the inside.
The deck was spotless, no streaks, no spilled oil.
Coiled ropes were stacked as neatly as in a catalog.
I walked into the accommodation block,
the corridor lights were on.
Every cabin door was open and every bed was made.
In the mess hall, 22 plates sat on the tables,
hot food, steam still rising.
In the galley, a kettle was whistling.
I turned it off and touched the teapot.
Warm, somebody had been here minutes ago,
Maybe seconds. I shouted:
Coast Guard inspection, is anyone aboard?
Nothing, only the hum of the generators.
Then I saw the whiteboard beside the galley door.
Black marker, block letters, written in a hurry.
Count the crew every hour.
If the number changes, do not say it out loud.
Under it, someone had written a tally.
22 lines and a 23rd line scratched out so hard
the marker had torn the board.
I didn't believe in ghosts,
I believed in missing paperwork.
So I did what an inspector does.
I found the crew manifest in the captain's office
and began checking names against faces.
Passport photos were pinned in a row on the wall.
22 crew, Captain Murrow, the chief engineer,
the cook, the bosun, the deck hands.
At 7 p.m. I heard the first sound
that wasn't machinery, a bell.
I followed it down to the mess hall
and they were all there.
22 men and women sitting in silence, facing the door.
Nobody was eating, nobody blinked.
The plates in front of them were empty now.
I counted, one, two, three, all the way to 22.
I'm Inspector Reeve, I said, you're all safe.
The Coast Guard is, the captain stood up.
His voice was calm, almost kind.
Inspector, he said, you are late for the count.
And then all 22 of them turned to look
at the empty chair at the end of the table.
I asked what they meant, nobody answered.
The captain only said, sit down please.
I didn't sit, I backed toward the door and counted again.
22 plus me, 23.
That was the number the transponder had been broadcasting.
Which one of you boarded late?
I asked, who isn't on the manifest?
The cook, a thin man with a burned scar across his wrist,
shook his head very slowly.
Nobody is missing from the manifest, he whispered.
I looked at the empty chair,
a name card sat in front of it face down.
I turned it over with one finger.
The card was blank, the captain spoke again.
It is 7:15, ask us again at eight.
Then all 22 stood up at the same moment
and walked out of the mess hall,
past me, without touching me, without looking at me.
The door closed behind them.
I stood alone with 22 empty plates.
My first theory was simple.
The crew had been exposed to something,
carbon monoxide maybe.
Gas from the cargo tanks,
it makes people calm, obedient, sluggish.
I'd read reports like that.
I pulled the gas detectors from the bridge cabinet
and walked the ship.
Everything read clean.
At 8 p.m., the bell rang again.
This time, I went to the mess hall first
and stood near the door, counting as they entered.
I counted aloud quietly.
20, 21, 22, the doors closed.
I turned around and my stomach dropped.
The captain was looking at me.
Inspector, he said, how many are in the room?
I remembered the whiteboard.
If the number changes, do not say it out loud.
I looked at the chairs, 22 crew members, me,
standing near the door, 23.
But the table had 24 chairs. 22, I lied.
The captain smiled
and it was the worst thing I'd seen all night.
Good, he said.
Last time, the inspector said 23.
I locked myself on the bridge and opened the ship's log.
The first pages were normal, speed, weather, fuel.
Then on day four, the handwriting changed.
The entries became shorter.
Day four, count 22. Day five, count 22.
Day six, inspector boarded, count 23.
Day six, inspector said the number aloud.
Count 22. I flipped back.
The same line appeared again on day seven, day eight, day nine.
A different date each time, but always the same note.
Inspector boarded.
Every few days, a helicopter
had dropped an inspector on deck
and every time the count had gone back to 22.
My hands were shaking.
I looked at the handwriting.
The slanted R, the cross T, the same way I cross mine.
I checked the signature at the bottom of the last page.
D. Reeve, I hadn't written any of it.
At 9 p.m., I opened the captain's safe.
Inside was a second manifest.
The original, the one filed
before the ship left Rotterdam.
It wasn't 22 names, it was 23.
The last name, handwritten at the bottom,
Daniel Reeve, third officer.
Beside it, a passport photo.
My face, my hair, a little longer.
A uniform I'd never worn.
Below the photo, a note.
Lost overboard, day one.
Replaced by inspector.
Replacement removed from count
and then I understood the rule on the whiteboard.
The crew didn't count themselves.
They counted me.
Every hour they checked
whether the ship had taken me back yet.
The captain was standing in the doorway.
You came aboard in a helicopter, inspector,
he said gently.
But you were never in the helicopter.
You were in the water.
I ran to the deck.
The helicopter was gone.
The horizon was empty.
Black water in every direction.
At 10 p.m., I heard the bell again.
This time, I walked to the mess hall on my own.
22 crew sitting in their places
and one empty chair I looked at the plates.
23, I looked at my own hands.
They were wet, though I hadn't touched water in hours.
The deck under my boots was dripping, count the captain said.
I sat down in the chair
and for the first time that night, nobody flinched.
23, I said.
The ship's engines roared to life
and the lights flickered.
All around me, the crew exhaled
like people who had been holding their breath for years.
Outside, through the porthole,
I could see the distant lights
of a helicopter circling for a landing.
Someone was about to board.
A new inspector, young, nervous with a clipboard.
I stood up, took a black marker
and walked to the whiteboard in the galley.
I wrote the rule, the same one I'd read when I arrived.
Block letters, my handwriting.
Count the crew every hour.
If the number changes, do not say it out loud.
Then I turned to the door
because I could hear boots on the deck.
Inspector, I said, as the newcomer stepped inside,
you're late for the count.
